latest_nl_proof:
Fix integers m and g with m >= 2 and g >= 0, and define K_{m,g} as in the statement.

We will prove the more precise claim stated there.

Let x = (x_1,\dots,x_{m-1}) be any element of K_{m,g}. By definition of K_{m,g}, x is a tuple of positive integers. Therefore, for every r in {1,\dots,m-1}, we have
x_r >= 1.

Also by definition of K_{m,g},
x_1 + \cdots + x_{m-1} = g.
Since each x_k is a positive integer, in particular each x_k is nonnegative, so for any fixed r we have
x_r <= x_1 + \cdots + x_{m-1} = g.
Hence for every r in {1,\dots,m-1},
1 <= x_r <= g.
This proves the coordinatewise bound claimed for every x in K_{m,g}.

Now suppose g >= 1. Let x in K_{m,g}. From the bound just proved, each coordinate x_r belongs to {1,\dots,g}. Therefore
x = (x_1,\dots,x_{m-1}) \in {1,\dots,g}^{m-1}.
Since x was arbitrary, we obtain
K_{m,g} \subseteq {1,\dots,g}^{m-1}.
The set {1,\dots,g} is finite, so its Cartesian power {1,\dots,g}^{m-1} is finite. Therefore K_{m,g}, being a subset of a finite set, is finite.

Now suppose g = 0. If x were in K_{m,0}, then each coordinate x_r would be a positive integer, hence x_r >= 1 for all r. Since m >= 2, there is at least one coordinate (indeed m-1 >= 1), and thus
x_1 + \cdots + x_{m-1} >= m-1 >= 1,
which contradicts the defining condition
x_1 + \cdots + x_{m-1} = 0.
So no such x exists, and therefore
K_{m,0} = \emptyset.
In particular, K_{m,0} is finite.

Thus in all cases K_{m,g} is finite. More precisely, every x in K_{m,g} satisfies 1 <= x_r <= g for each r in {1,\dots,m-1}; hence if g >= 1 then K_{m,g} \subseteq {1,\dots,g}^{m-1}, and if g = 0 then K_{m,g} = \emptyset, exactly as claimed.
role_in_parent: Supplies the finiteness hypotheses required before applying the injection-implies-cardinality-inequality principle.
statement_nl: Let m be an integer with m >= 2 and let g be an integer with g >= 0. Define K_{m,g} to be the set of all tuples x = (x_1,...,x_{m-1}) of positive integers such that for all i,j in {1,...,m-1}, if i + j < m then x_i + x_j >= x_{i+j}, and if i + j > m then x_i + x_j + 1 >= x_{i+j-m}, and such that x_1 + ... + x_{m-1} = g. Then K_{m,g} is finite. More precisely, every tuple x in K_{m,g} satisfies 1 <= x_r <= g for each r in {1,...,m-1}; hence if g >= 1 then K_{m,g} is contained in the finite box {1,...,g}^{m-1}, and if g = 0 then K_{m,g} is empty.

domain_restrictions: m is an integer with m ≥ 2
g is an integer with g ≥ 0
K_{m,g} consists of tuples x = (x_1,...,x_{m-1}) with each x_k a positive integer
Inequality case 1: for all i,j, if i + j < m then x_i + x_j ≥ x_{i+j}
Inequality case 2: for all i,j, if i + j > m then x_i + x_j + 1 ≥ x_{i+j-m}
No explicit inequality requirement is stated for the case i + j = m (indices excluded from both case conditions)
statement_semantic_sketch.normalized_claim: For all integers m ≥ 2 and g ≥ 0, let K_{m,g} = { x ∈ Z_{>0}^{m-1} : (x_1+...+x_{m-1}=g) ∧ (∀ i,j ∈ {1,...,m-1}, (i+j<m ⇒ x_i+x_j ≥ x_{i+j}) ∧ (i+j>m ⇒ x_i+x_j+1 ≥ x_{i+j-m})) }. Then for every x ∈ K_{m,g} and every r ∈ {1,...,m-1}, one has 1 ≤ x_r ≤ g. Consequently, if g ≥ 1 then K_{m,g} ⊆ {1,...,g}^{m-1} (hence finite), and if g = 0 then K_{m,0} = ∅.
quantifier_order: and then (case split) if g ≥ 1: K_{m,g} ⊆ {1,...,g}^{m-1}; if g = 0: K_{m,g} = ∅

variables.name: m
variables.role: global parameter (length of tuple is m-1)

witness_dependencies: No existential witnesses are introduced in the claim; K_{m,g} is defined by universal constraints on x and an equality constraint on the sum.
The asserted bounds 1 ≤ x_r ≤ g depend on membership x ∈ K_{m,g} (which includes both positivity and the sum-to-g constraint).
